title: Medical Ethics and Law
tagline: Ethical principles, consent and capacity, confidentiality, end-of-life decisions, research ethics and professionalism
summary: Medicine raises hard questions about what should be done, not only what can be done. This course covers the principles and theories of medical ethics, consent and mental capacity, confidentiality, ethical and legal questions at the beginning and end of life, justice and resource allocation, research ethics, and professionalism and regulation, following the law of England and Wales and noting where other countries differ.
overview: Clinical decisions are rarely only technical. Whether to admit a patient who refuses, whether to tell a relative about a genetic result, whether to start or stop a ventilator, who gets the last intensive care bed: each mixes evidence with values. Medical ethics offers methods for these decisions: the four principles of respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice, the moral theories behind them, and a structured way of working through a case that gets the facts right before arguing about values.

The course then applies these tools. It covers valid consent and the Montgomery duty to disclose material risks; capacity, best interests and advance decisions under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; the duty of confidentiality and when information may or must be shared; abortion, prenatal screening, assisted conception and decisions about newborns; withdrawing treatment, resuscitation decisions, palliative sedation and the assisted dying debate; QALYs, cost-effectiveness and fair process in resource allocation; the history and requirements of research ethics; and the professional duties of doctors and how they are regulated.

The law described is that of England and Wales as of 2026, with the main cases and statutes named and dated, and the GMC's current guidance. Scotland, Northern Ireland and other countries differ in important ways, and the law changes, as recent reforms of abortion law and debates on assisted dying show. The law is presented to explain how decisions are made, not as legal advice. Every chapter uses fictional clinical cases worked step by step, quick checks, and exercises with full answers.
outcomes: Apply the four principles and the main moral theories to a clinical dilemma, using specification and balancing, and set out the reasoning in a structured way.
Explain the requirements of valid consent, including the Montgomery test of material risk, and communicate risk using absolute numbers and natural frequencies.
Assess decision-making capacity using the functional test of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and describe best-interests decisions, advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting powers of attorney.
Describe the legal and ethical basis of confidentiality, and decide when information may be disclosed with consent, by legal requirement or in the public interest.
Summarise the law on abortion and assisted conception in Great Britain, and discuss the ethics of moral status, prenatal screening and decisions about newborn infants.
Analyse decisions to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment and about CPR, distinguish palliative sedation from euthanasia, and outline the law and arguments on assisted dying.
Calculate and interpret QALYs and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, and evaluate allocation decisions against theories of justice and fair process.
State the requirements of ethical research, including equipoise, consent and its exceptions, independent review and transparency, and relate them to the history of research abuses.
Describe how doctors are regulated in the UK, the duties of candour and of raising concerns, and the standards of probity and professional boundaries.

history.title: The Hippocratic Oath
history.detail: The Hippocratic Oath, probably written in the 5th or 4th century BCE, binds physicians to help the sick, to avoid harm and injustice, and to keep secret what they learn in treating patients.

history.title: Percival's Medical Ethics
history.detail: Thomas Percival, a Manchester physician, publishes Medical Ethics, a code of professional conduct for hospital doctors that shapes later codes in Britain and the United States.

history.title: The General Medical Council
history.detail: The Medical Act 1858 creates the General Medical Council and a register of qualified practitioners, beginning statutory regulation of the medical profession in the UK.

history.title: The Nuremberg Code
history.detail: After the trial of Nazi doctors, the judges set out ten principles for permissible human experimentation, beginning with the statement that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.

history.title: The Declaration of Helsinki
history.detail: The World Medical Association adopts its ethical principles for medical research involving people. Revised many times, most recently in 2024, it remains the main international code for research ethics.

history.title: Beecher exposes unethical research
history.detail: Henry Beecher, an anaesthetist at Harvard, publishes 22 examples of ethically questionable studies from mainstream research in the New England Journal of Medicine.

history.title: Principles and the Belmont Report
history.detail: Tom Beauchamp and James Childress publish Principles of Biomedical Ethics, and the US National Commission issues the Belmont Report, setting out respect for persons, beneficence and justice in research.

history.title: Gillick
history.detail: In Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority, the House of Lords holds that a child under 16 with sufficient understanding and intelligence can consent to medical treatment.

history.title: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland
history.detail: The House of Lords holds that tube feeding is medical treatment and may lawfully be withdrawn from Anthony Bland, in a persistent vegetative state, because continuing it is no longer in his best interests.

history.title: Montgomery
history.detail: The UK Supreme Court rules in Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board that doctors must ensure patients are aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives, replacing the Bolam test for disclosure of risk.

references.title: Principles of Biomedical Ethics
references.authors: Tom L. Beauchamp and James F. Childress
references.note: Eighth edition. The classic account of the four principles, with chapters on moral status, autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice and professional relationships.

references.title: Medical Ethics and Law: A Curriculum for the 21st Century
references.authors: Dominic Wilkinson, Jonathan Herring and Julian Savulescu
references.note: Third edition. A UK textbook organised around the medical ethics and law curriculum, with clinical cases and the law of England and Wales.

references.title: Medical Law and Ethics
references.note: Tenth edition. A detailed and readable account of English medical law, including consent, capacity, confidentiality, reproduction, end of life and resource allocation.

references.title: Clinical Ethics: A Practical Approach to Ethical Decisions in Clinical Medicine
references.authors: Albert R. Jonsen, Mark Siegler and William J. Winslade
references.note: Ninth edition. The source of the four-topics method for analysing clinical ethics cases.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: The professional standards for doctors in the UK, in effect from 30 January 2024, with linked guidance on decision making and consent (2020), confidentiality (2017) and treatment and care towards the end of life.

references.title: Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice
references.note: Statutory guidance on the principles of the Mental Capacity Act, assessing capacity, best interests, advance decisions, lasting powers of attorney and research involving adults who lack capacity.

references.title: Declaration of Helsinki: Ethical Principles for Medical Research Involving Human Participants
references.note: The current revision of the main international code for research ethics, adopted in October 2024.
